result:
When you tell someone "write freely about whatever you want," you get to see what has been quietly sitting in the back of their mind waiting for permission to come out.

What has been sitting in the back of my mind is this: we are obsessed with beginnings and almost completely blind to middles.

We love launches, announcements, grand openings, first drafts, first steps, founding stories. We cut ribbons. We have entire industries and aesthetics built around starting things. The startup. The debut novel. The New Year. The blank notebook on January 1st.

Almost nobody wants to write about maintenance.

And maintenance is where almost all of life actually happens.

Consider a single city block. Someone, at some point, had the exciting job of designing it. There were blueprints and renderings and a mayor with a big pair of scissors. Photos in the local paper. That took maybe two years.

Then for the next hundred years, someone had to maintain it. Sweep the sidewalk. Repaint the crosswalk lines every spring after the snowplows chew them up. Unclog the storm drain that gets full of maple helicopters every October. Replace the one flickering streetlight that buzzes. Tighten the bolts on the park bench. The block exists not because it was once built, but because ten thousand small, invisible acts of care keep rebuilding it every single day.

We don't have a word that makes maintenance sound heroic. In English, maintenance is what you do to a car you don't really love anymore before you trade it in. The person who maintains is a janitor, a super, a sysadmin, the night shift. Our mythology is all about the hunter, not the person who preserves the meat; the author, not the librarian who keeps the book from molding.

But I think we are living through a quiet crisis of maintenance, and it's why so many things feel brittle right now.

There's a concept in software called technical debt. You take a shortcut when you build something quickly - you write messy code that works for now, promising yourself you'll clean it up later. Later never comes. That debt accrues interest. Eventually you spend more time fighting the mess you made than you would have spent doing it right.

We now have infrastructural debt, ecological debt, attentional debt, relational debt.

We know how to start podcasts. We don't know how to keep one going to episode 200 when only 43 people are listening and your co-host is tired. We know how to fall in love. We are much less fluent in what love looks like on a random Tuesday in year seven when no one is sick or celebrating and you have to decide what to have for dinner again and still be kind. We know how to join a gym in January. We don't know how to keep showing up in March.

We treat the middle as failure. If you're not growing, you're dying. If it's not new, it's not news. And so we keep abandoning things in the middle to go start something new, where we can feel competent and exciting again.

A friend of mine works for the National Park Service. She doesn't design new parks. Her whole job is trail maintenance in the same 12-mile stretch in Washington. She moves rocks. She digs drainage. She puts up a little sign that says "please stay on trail." She has done this for nine years. I asked her once if she gets bored. She said, "No. The trail is never the same trail. The water is different every spring. People cut a new shortcut every summer. My job is to have a relationship with this place, not to finish it."

That phrase has stuck with me. A relationship, not a finish line.

We are taught to think of work as something with a finish line. Essay due. Project shipped. Degree earned. But the most important things don't have finish lines. Your health doesn't get "finished." Your friendships don't get finished. Your curiosity doesn't get finished. The street you live on never gets finished.

If you reframe life as maintenance, it changes everything.

For example, boredom. We treat boredom as a bug to be patched with more stimulation. Scroll faster. New show. But boredom might be the feeling you get right before you actually notice something. It's the clearing. My favorite writers have all described the same thing: staring at the wall for an hour before the sentence comes. The wall-staring was the work. The boredom was maintenance of attention.

Attention is perhaps the most poorly maintained infrastructure we have. We understand physical fitness - you have to keep moving your body or it atrophies. But attention is a muscle too. And we are feeding it ultra-processed junk. Every app is designed to start something new: new video, new outrage, new sale, new notification. None of them are designed to help you sustain one thought for twenty minutes without switching.

So what does attention maintenance look like? It's not sexy. It looks like reading one book slowly, even when you want to check your phone. It looks like listening to one person talk without rehearsing your response. It looks like watching the same tree out your window every morning for a month and noticing how it actually changes. It looks like letting a thought be unfinished.

I think about libraries a lot. A library is a maintenance building. Almost nothing new happens there. The point is to keep old things accessible. Someone has to keep dusting Shakespeare. Someone has to reshelve the books people put back in the wrong place. Someone has to repair the spine that cracked. It is deeply un-innovative. And it is civilization.

If we celebrated maintenance the way we celebrate invention, how would we talk differently? We would interview the person who has kept a community garden alive for 18 years, not just the kid who made an app to map community gardens. We would have awards for the line cook who has made perfect eggs for twenty years at the diner. We would ask couples who have been married for 40 years not "what's your secret?" as if it's a trick, but "what did you have to keep repairing?"

There is dignity in repetition when repetition is chosen.

I know this essay is supposed to be 1000 words of free writing, and I have not told you what I ate for breakfast or what my dreams are about. But this is what freedom feels like to me right now: the freedom to not invent something new, but to say, look at what is already here and is being held together by invisible thread.

Tomorrow morning, someone will wake up at 4 a.m. to salt roads before anyone else is awake. Someone will restart a server you rely on and never think about. Someone will pick up your trash. Someone will text a friend just to check in, for no reason, for the tenth year in a row. None of that will trend.

If you want a small experiment: pick one thing you already have and maintain it on purpose for one week. Not improve. Not optimize. Not grow hack. Just maintain at its current level with care. Wash the same coffee mug every day and dry it. Water one plant. Reread one poem every evening. Respond to one old message. Sweep your own block.

Notice how quickly your mind tries to turn it into a project with a goal. Notice how hard it is to just tend.

That resistance is the interesting part. That resistance is where we forgot how to be.

We don't need more beginnings. We need more people willing to stay.
